lines.text: Earth, with the Sun away to the left. Look at the line down the middle: lit on one side, dark on the other. That line is the terminator.
lines.spoken: Earth, with the Sun away to the left. Look at the line down the middle: lit on one side, dark on the other. That line is the terminator.

lines.text: Now the clock runs at one hour every second. Watch the cities ride round — none of them is standing still.
lines.spoken: Now the clock runs at one hour every second. Watch the cities ride round, none of them is standing still.

lines.text: Kathmandu is moving towards the dark side. For the people there, the Sun is sinking lower in the west.
lines.spoken: Kathmandu is moving towards the dark side. For the people there, the Sun is sinking lower in the west.

lines.text: And now it’s night in Nepal. Nothing turned off — their patch of ground simply swung round to the far side of the planet from the Sun.
lines.spoken: And now it’s night in Nepal. Nothing turned off, their patch of ground simply swung round to the far side of the planet from the Sun.

lines.text: Meanwhile New York is rolling into the sunlight. Somewhere on Earth, someone is always watching a sunrise.
lines.spoken: Meanwhile New York is rolling into the sunlight. Somewhere on Earth, someone is always watching a sunrise.

lines.text: Twenty-four seconds here, twenty-four hours there. One spin: one day.
lines.spoken: Twenty-four seconds here, twenty-four hours there. One spin: one day.

lines.text: Notice the dividing line never moved relative to the Sun. Only the ground moved past it.
lines.spoken: Notice the dividing line never moved relative to the Sun. Only the ground moved past it.

lines.text: Nepal is facing the Sun square on: local noon.
lines.spoken: Nepal is facing the Sun square on: local noon.

lines.text: Eleven hours later the same thing happens in New York.
lines.spoken: Eleven hours later the same thing happens in New York.

lines.text: From above the North Pole: Earth turning anticlockwise, which carries you eastwards.
lines.spoken: From above the North Pole: Earth turning anticlockwise, which carries you eastwards.

lines.text: Now we’re holding station 2,600 km directly above Kathmandu, moving along with the ground. It’s the middle of the night down there.
lines.spoken: Now we’re holding station 2,600 kilometres directly above Kathmandu, moving along with the ground. It’s the middle of the night down there.

lines.text: One hour a second. Look towards the horizon on the left — something is coming.
lines.spoken: One hour a second. Look towards the horizon on the left, something is coming.

lines.text: There it is: the terminator, arriving. On the ground this is dawn, and it is crossing the country at well over 1,000 km/h.
lines.spoken: There it is: the terminator, arriving. On the ground this is dawn, and it is crossing the country at well over 1,000 kilometres per hour.

lines.text: Full daylight now, and the Sun climbing. It’s the longest day of the year down there — the June solstice.
lines.spoken: Full daylight now, and the Sun climbing. It’s the longest day of the year down there, the June solstice.

lines.text: And the far edge arrives. Sunset. The same line, on the other side of the planet from where we met it this morning.
lines.spoken: And the far edge arrives. Sunset. The same line, on the other side of the planet from where we met it this morning.

lines.text: One full turn, one sunrise, one sunset. Do that 365 times and you’ve gone round the Sun — which is the next lesson.
lines.spoken: One full turn, one sunrise, one sunset. Do that 365 times and you’ve gone round the Sun, which is the next lesson.

lines.text: In June the North Pole never leaves the sunlight — the Sun just circles round without setting.
lines.spoken: In June the North Pole never leaves the sunlight, the Sun just circles round without setting.

lines.text: And on the same date, the South Pole never sees the Sun at all.
lines.spoken: And on the same date, the South Pole never sees the Sun at all.

lines.text: This is Earth on 8 April 2024, seen from where the Moon was — about 370,000 km away. It’s mid-afternoon in America. Nothing has happened yet.
lines.spoken: This is Earth on 8 April 2024, seen from where the Moon was, about 370,000 kilometres away. It’s mid-afternoon in America. Nothing has happened yet.

lines.text: Now the clock runs at ten minutes every second. Watch the Pacific coast of Mexico for a small dark dot.
lines.spoken: Now the clock runs at ten minutes every second. Watch the Pacific coast of Mexico for a small dark dot.

lines.text: There it is. That dot is the umbra: the part of the shadow where the Moon blocks the Sun completely. It is only about 200 km across.
lines.spoken: There it is. That dot is the umbra: the part of the shadow where the Moon blocks the Sun completely. It is only about 200 kilometres across.

lines.text: It’s racing north-east at over 2,000 km/h — faster than a jet. Anyone standing under it gets about four minutes of darkness, then it’s gone.
lines.spoken: It’s racing north-east at over 2,000 kilometres per hour, faster than a jet. Anyone standing under it gets about four minutes of darkness, then it’s gone.

lines.text: Around 18:17 UTC the shadow is closest to the middle of Earth. Everything shaded around the dot is the penumbra — those millions of people see a partial eclipse.
lines.spoken: Around 18 17 U T C the shadow is closest to the middle of Earth. Everything shaded around the dot is the penumbra, those millions of people see a partial eclipse.

lines.text: Now it crosses eastern Canada and heads out over the Atlantic.
lines.spoken: Now it crosses eastern Canada and heads out over the Atlantic.

lines.text: And it’s gone. Three hours, one thin ribbon of totality drawn across a planet.
lines.spoken: And it’s gone. Three hours, one thin ribbon of totality drawn across a planet.

lines.text: The umbra first touches Earth over the Pacific, near Mazatlán.
lines.spoken: The umbra first touches Earth over the Pacific, near Mazatlán.

lines.text: The shadow crossing Texas. Dallas had 3 minutes 51 seconds of totality.
lines.spoken: The shadow crossing Texas. Dallas had 3 minutes 51 seconds of totality.

lines.text: From the side: Sun, Moon and Earth in one straight line.
lines.spoken: From the side: Sun, Moon and Earth in one straight line.

lines.text: You’re standing in Dallas, looking up through a narrow, telescope-like view. The Moon has already taken a bite out of the Sun.
lines.spoken: You’re standing in Dallas, looking up through a narrow, telescope-like view. The Moon has already taken a bite out of the Sun.

lines.text: Ten minutes a second. Watch the Sun shrink to a crescent — and look at how much daylight is left. Still plenty, even with the Sun 70% covered.
lines.spoken: Ten minutes a second. Watch the Sun shrink to a crescent, and look at how much daylight is left. Still plenty, even with the Sun 70 percent covered.

lines.text: Slowing down to one minute a second. The last sliver of Sun is about to vanish.
lines.spoken: Slowing down to one minute a second. The last sliver of Sun is about to vanish.

lines.text: Totality. The Moon covers the Sun completely, and the corona appears — the Sun’s million-degree outer atmosphere, invisible any other time.
lines.spoken: Totality. The Moon covers the Sun completely, and the corona appears, the Sun’s million-degree outer atmosphere, invisible any other time.

lines.text: Pull back and look at the sky itself. In the middle of the afternoon it has gone twilight-dark, all the way to the horizon.
lines.spoken: Pull back and look at the sky itself. In the middle of the afternoon it has gone twilight-dark, all the way to the horizon.

lines.text: Three minutes fifty-one seconds in Dallas, and then the first sliver of Sun returns — the diamond ring. Glasses back on.
lines.spoken: Three minutes fifty-one seconds in Dallas, and then the first sliver of Sun returns, the diamond ring. Glasses back on.

lines.text: Another hour and a quarter and it’s over. Somewhere under the shadow’s path, somebody is already planning their next one.
lines.spoken: Another hour and a quarter and it’s over. Somewhere under the shadow’s path, somebody is already planning their next one.

lines.text: Use the Jump to buttons to compare this with a ring of fire.
lines.spoken: Use the Jump to buttons to compare this with a ring of fire.

lines.text: The corona, with the Moon’s disc dead centre.
lines.spoken: The corona, with the Moon’s disc dead centre.

lines.text: An annular eclipse over the South Pacific: the Moon is too far away to cover the Sun, so a ring of light survives.
lines.spoken: An annular eclipse over the South Pacific: the Moon is too far away to cover the Sun, so a ring of light survives.

lines.text: A partial eclipse seen from Northern Ireland: the umbra misses Earth entirely, so this is the most anyone saw.
lines.spoken: A partial eclipse seen from Northern Ireland: the umbra misses Earth entirely, so this is the most anyone saw.

lines.text: The whole sky at mid-totality.
lines.spoken: The whole sky at mid-totality.

lines.text: The Moon, close up, a few hours before the eclipse of 14 March 2025. Fully lit — this is a full moon, which is exactly what a lunar eclipse needs.
lines.spoken: The Moon, close up, a few hours before the eclipse of 14 March 2025. Fully lit, this is a full moon, which is exactly what a lunar eclipse needs.

lines.text: Earth is behind us, between the Moon and the Sun. Its shadow stretches out into space, and the Moon is drifting straight into it.
lines.spoken: Earth is behind us, between the Moon and the Sun. Its shadow stretches out into space, and the Moon is drifting straight into it.

lines.text: The edge of Earth’s umbra starts creeping across the surface. Unlike a solar eclipse, this takes hours and the whole night side of Earth can watch.
lines.spoken: The edge of Earth’s umbra starts creeping across the surface. Unlike a solar eclipse, this takes hours and the whole night side of Earth can watch.

lines.text: Nearly swallowed. Notice the colour arriving — it isn’t going black.
lines.spoken: Nearly swallowed. Notice the colour arriving, it isn’t going black.

lines.text: Totality. The Moon glows copper red, lit only by sunlight bent through Earth’s atmosphere — every sunrise and sunset on the planet, focused onto one rock.
lines.spoken: Totality. The Moon glows copper red, lit only by sunlight bent through Earth’s atmosphere, every sunrise and sunset on the planet, focused onto one rock.

lines.text: Now turn round and look back from the Moon’s position: Earth is a black disc exactly covering the Sun, ringed with the glow of its own atmosphere.
lines.spoken: Now turn round and look back from the Moon’s position: Earth is a black disc exactly covering the Sun, ringed with the glow of its own atmosphere.

lines.text: Totality lasted 65 minutes. Then the Moon slides back out into full sunlight.
lines.spoken: Totality lasted 65 minutes. Then the Moon slides back out into full sunlight.

lines.text: Greatest eclipse: the Moon deepest inside Earth’s umbra.
lines.spoken: Greatest eclipse: the Moon deepest inside Earth’s umbra.

lines.text: What you’d see standing on the Moon: Earth eclipsing the Sun.
lines.spoken: What you’d see standing on the Moon: Earth eclipsing the Sun.

lines.text: Sun, Earth, Moon in a line — the opposite order from a solar eclipse.
lines.spoken: Sun, Earth, Moon in a line, the opposite order from a solar eclipse.

lines.text: The eclipse of 7 September 2025 — 82 minutes of totality, seen across Asia, Africa and Europe.
lines.spoken: The eclipse of 7 September 2025, 82 minutes of totality, seen across Asia, Africa and Europe.

lines.text: Back to Earth seen from the Moon — but now at the new moon of 11 January 2024. The Moon is between us and the Sun, exactly as it was in April. So where is the shadow?
lines.spoken: Back to Earth seen from the Moon, but now at the new moon of 11 January 2024. The Moon is between us and the Sun, exactly as it was in April. So where is the shadow?

lines.text: Nowhere. The Moon’s orbit is tilted, so this month the shadow sails past, thousands of kilometres clear of the planet.
lines.spoken: Nowhere. The Moon’s orbit is tilted, so this month the shadow sails past, thousands of kilometres clear of the planet.

lines.text: Next new moon, four weeks later. Still a miss — though not by quite as much.
lines.spoken: Next new moon, four weeks later. Still a miss, though not by quite as much.

lines.text: March. Closer again. The tilted orbit is swinging the Moon down towards the Earth–Sun line.
lines.spoken: March. Closer again. The tilted orbit is swinging the Moon down towards the Earth–Sun line.

lines.text: 8 April. This time the new moon lands right on the line — the Moon is at a node — and the shadow finally lands. That’s the eclipse you watched at the start of the lesson.
lines.spoken: 8 April. This time the new moon lands right on the line, the Moon is at a node, and the shadow finally lands. That’s the eclipse you watched at the start of the lesson.

lines.text: One month later it has sailed straight past the node, and the shadow misses again — this time on the other side.
lines.spoken: One month later it has sailed straight past the node, and the shadow misses again, this time on the other side.

lines.text: June: missing by even more. The hoop of the Moon’s orbit keeps pointing the same way in space while Earth travels round the Sun, so the line-up only comes back round about every six months.
lines.spoken: June: missing by even more. The hoop of the Moon’s orbit keeps pointing the same way in space while Earth travels round the Sun, so the line-up only comes back round about every six months.

lines.text: And there it is — the next eclipse season, six months on. Six new moons for one eclipse.
lines.spoken: And there it is, the next eclipse season, six months on. Six new moons for one eclipse.

lines.text: The same moment from the side: Moon exactly on the line from Earth to the Sun.
lines.spoken: The same moment from the side: Moon exactly on the line from Earth to the Sun.

lines.where: tilt jump "Edge on, a month earlier"
lines.text: A month earlier, from the side: the Moon rides well off the line.
lines.spoken: A month earlier, from the side: the Moon rides well off the line.

lines.text: Home. Everyone you’ve ever heard of lived down there. Let’s find out where “there” is.
lines.spoken: Home. Everyone you’ve ever heard of lived down there. Let’s find out where “there” is.

lines.text: The Solar System from above: the Sun and eight planets, about 9 billion kilometres across. Light crosses it in roughly eight hours.
lines.spoken: The Solar System from above: the Sun and eight planets, about 9 billion kilometres across. Light crosses it in roughly eight hours.

lines.text: Now we jump out 150,000 light-years. This is our galaxy, the Milky Way, from above. That whole Solar System is far too small to see here. It’s at the orange label.
lines.spoken: Now we jump out 150,000 light-years. This is our galaxy, the Milky Way, from above. That whole Solar System is far too small to see here. It’s at the orange label.

lines.text: Between 100 and 400 billion stars. The Sun takes about 230 million years to go round the centre once. The last time it was where it is now, the first dinosaurs were just appearing.
lines.spoken: Between 100 and 400 billion stars. The Sun takes about 230 million years to go round the centre once. The last time it was where it is now, the first dinosaurs were just appearing.

lines.text: From the side it’s a thin disc with a bulge in the middle. We live inside that disc, so looking along it from Earth we see a band of light across the sky. That band is what we call the Milky Way.
lines.spoken: From the side it’s a thin disc with a bulge in the middle. We live inside that disc, so looking along it from Earth we see a band of light across the sky. That band is what we call the Milky Way.

lines.text: Every star you’ve ever seen with your own eyes is in here, most of them within a few thousand light-years of the Sun.
lines.spoken: Every star you’ve ever seen with your own eyes is in here, most of them within a few thousand light-years of the Sun.

lines.where: home jump "The middle of the galaxy"
lines.text: The central bar and bulge. At the very centre is Sagittarius A*, a black hole of about 4 million Suns.
lines.spoken: The central bar and bulge. At the very centre is Sagittarius A*, a black hole of about 4 million Suns.

lines.text: The Large Magellanic Cloud, 163,000 light-years away, a small galaxy circling ours. From the southern hemisphere you can see it with your own eyes, like a torn-off scrap of the Milky Way.
lines.spoken: The Large Magellanic Cloud, 163,000 light-years away, a small galaxy circling ours. From the southern hemisphere you can see it with your own eyes, like a torn-off scrap of the Milky Way.

lines.text: The Andromeda Galaxy, 2.5 million light-years away. It’s the biggest galaxy near us, with around a trillion stars, and the most distant thing you can see without a telescope.
lines.spoken: The Andromeda Galaxy, 2.5 million light-years away. It’s the biggest galaxy near us, with around a trillion stars, and the most distant thing you can see without a telescope.

lines.text: Andromeda is heading our way at about 110 kilometres per second. A few billion years from now, it and the Milky Way will probably merge into one giant galaxy.
lines.spoken: Andromeda is heading our way at about 110 kilometres per second. A few billion years from now, it and the Milky Way will probably merge into one giant galaxy.

lines.text: Much further out, the Whirlpool Galaxy, 31 million light-years away. It was the first galaxy anyone saw spiral arms in, back in 1845. A smaller galaxy is tugging on it.
lines.spoken: Much further out, the Whirlpool Galaxy, 31 million light-years away. It was the first galaxy anyone saw spiral arms in, back in 1845. A smaller galaxy is tugging on it.

lines.text: And Messier 87, 53 million light-years away, a giant ball of a trillion old stars. In 2019 its central black hole became the first ever photographed.
lines.spoken: And Messier 87, 53 million light-years away, a giant ball of a trillion old stars. In 2019 its central black hole became the first ever photographed.

lines.text: That black hole weighs as much as six and a half billion Suns, and it blasts out a jet of gas 5,000 light-years long at nearly the speed of light.
lines.spoken: That black hole weighs as much as six and a half billion Suns, and it blasts out a jet of gas 5,000 light-years long at nearly the speed of light.

lines.text: The light reaching us from it left 53 million years ago, not long after the dinosaurs died out.
lines.spoken: The light reaching us from it left 53 million years ago, not long after the dinosaurs died out.

lines.text: The Triangulum Galaxy, 2.7 million light-years away, the third big member of our Local Group.
lines.spoken: The Triangulum Galaxy, 2.7 million light-years away, the third big member of our Local Group.

lines.text: The Sombrero Galaxy, 31 million light-years away, seen almost edge-on.
lines.spoken: The Sombrero Galaxy, 31 million light-years away, seen almost edge-on.

lines.text: This grid is a way of picturing gravity. The Sun sits at the bottom of a deep well, and everything near it is on a slope leading down.
lines.spoken: This grid is a way of picturing gravity. The Sun sits at the bottom of a deep well, and everything near it is on a slope leading down.

lines.text: The clock runs at a week every second. Mercury, deep in the well, whips round in 88 days. Mars, higher up the slope, takes almost two years.
lines.spoken: The clock runs at a week every second. Mercury, deep in the well, whips round in 88 days. Mars, higher up the slope, takes almost two years.

lines.text: None of them slides down to the Sun. Each one is moving sideways fast enough to circle the well forever, like a marble rolling round a bowl.
lines.spoken: None of them slides down to the Sun. Each one is moving sideways fast enough to circle the well forever, like a marble rolling round a bowl.

lines.text: Backing out to the giant planets, at a month per second. Out here the slope is gentle, so Jupiter and Saturn amble round at a walking pace, for a planet.
lines.spoken: Backing out to the giant planets, at a month per second. Out here the slope is gentle, so Jupiter and Saturn amble round at a walking pace, for a planet.

lines.text: See the little dimples where the planets are? Each one has its own well too. We’ll look at those next.
lines.spoken: See the little dimples where the planets are? Each one has its own well too. We’ll look at those next.

lines.text: The real dent is far too slight to see. Even at the Sun’s surface it slows time by only about two parts in a million. But the shape is right.
lines.spoken: The real dent is far too slight to see. Even at the Sun’s surface it slows time by only about two parts in a million. But the shape is right.

lines.text: From directly above, the grid shows rings bunching up towards the Sun.
lines.spoken: From directly above, the grid shows rings bunching up towards the Sun.

lines.text: The same orbits without the grid. The motion is identical; the grid is only a picture.
lines.spoken: The same orbits without the grid. The motion is identical; the grid is only a picture.

lines.text: Earth’s own well, from 800,000 kilometres. It’s a tiny dimple next to the Sun’s, but it’s plenty deep enough to hold on to the Moon.
lines.spoken: Earth’s own well, from 800,000 kilometres. It’s a tiny dimple next to the Sun’s, but it’s plenty deep enough to hold on to the Moon.

lines.text: A day every second. The Moon rolls round the rim of Earth’s well once every 27 days. It’s falling towards us all the time, and missing.
lines.spoken: A day every second. The Moon rolls round the rim of Earth’s well once every 27 days. It’s falling towards us all the time, and missing.

lines.text: The Moon moves at only about 1 km per second, slow compared with the planets, because Earth’s well is so much shallower than the Sun’s.
lines.spoken: The Moon moves at only about 1 kilometres per second, slow compared with the planets, because Earth’s well is so much shallower than the Sun’s.

lines.text: Now Jupiter, which has 318 times Earth’s mass, so a far deeper well. Its four big moons circle inside it, Io fastest because it’s furthest down.
lines.spoken: Now Jupiter, which has 318 times Earth’s mass, so a far deeper well. Its four big moons circle inside it, Io fastest because it’s furthest down.

lines.text: A day per second. Same rule as the planets round the Sun: deeper in the well, faster you go.
lines.spoken: A day per second. Same rule as the planets round the Sun: deeper in the well, faster you go.

lines.text: Wells inside wells: moons round planets, planets round the Sun, and the Sun round the middle of the galaxy.
lines.spoken: Wells inside wells: moons round planets, planets round the Sun, and the Sun round the middle of the galaxy.

lines.text: Saturn’s well, with its ring of moons. Titan is the big one.
lines.spoken: Saturn’s well, with its ring of moons. Titan is the big one.

lines.text: This scene hands you the controls. Below the view you’ve got a flight console: destination, ship speed, flight clock, and an Engage button.
lines.spoken: This scene hands you the controls. Below the view you’ve got a flight console: destination, ship speed, flight clock, and an Engage button.

lines.text: Start easy. Set the destination to Moon, the ship speed to Speed of light, and the flight clock to Real time.
lines.spoken: Start easy. Set the destination to Moon, the ship speed to Speed of light, and the flight clock to Real time.

lines.text: Press Engage and time the trip. It takes 1.3 seconds — the only genuinely quick journey in the Solar System.
lines.spoken: Press Engage and time the trip. It takes 1.3 seconds, the only genuinely quick journey in the Solar System.

lines.text: Now try the Sun at light speed. Even at the universe’s speed limit, that’s 8 minutes 20 seconds. Use the flight clock to speed the waiting up.
lines.spoken: Now try the Sun at light speed. Even at the universe’s speed limit, that’s 8 minutes 20 seconds. Use the flight clock to speed the waiting up.

lines.text: Then pick Neptune, and change your ship speed to Voyager 1. Read the trip estimate before you launch. Then take a breath.
lines.spoken: Then pick Neptune, and change your ship speed to Voyager 1. Read the trip estimate before you launch. Then take a breath.

lines.text: Neptune, 4.5 billion km from the Sun. From here the Sun is just the brightest star in the sky.
lines.spoken: Neptune, 4.5 billion kilometres from the Sun. From here the Sun is just the brightest star in the sky.

lines.text: The Sun seen from Mercury’s distance — three times wider than we ever see it.
lines.spoken: The Sun seen from Mercury’s distance, three times wider than we ever see it.

lines.text: Earth from 14,000 km. Everything that has ever happened to anyone you have ever heard of happened down there.
lines.spoken: Earth from 14,000 kilometres. Everything that has ever happened to anyone you have ever heard of happened down there.

lines.text: Back out to 900,000 km and the Moon comes into frame. That gap is 384,400 km — you could fit every other planet in the Solar System into it, side by side, with room to spare.
lines.spoken: Back out to 900,000 kilometres and the Moon comes into frame. That gap is 384,400 kilometres, you could fit every other planet in the Solar System into it, side by side, with room to spare.

lines.text: Now from above the Sun, out to Mars. Earth is already just a dot on a ring. The Sun is 8 light-minutes away from it.
lines.spoken: Now from above the Sun, out to Mars. Earth is already just a dot on a ring. The Sun is 8 light-minutes away from it.

lines.text: Out past Jupiter and Saturn. Those four inner planets are now packed into the small bright area in the middle.
lines.spoken: Out past Jupiter and Saturn. Those four inner planets are now packed into the small bright area in the middle.

lines.text: And here is all of it: eight planets, 4.5 billion kilometres to Neptune, four hours at the speed of light.
lines.spoken: And here is all of it: eight planets, 4.5 billion kilometres to Neptune, four hours at the speed of light.

lines.text: Keep going and the planets vanish entirely. The Sun becomes one star among many — and the nearest of those is 7,000 times further away than Neptune.
lines.spoken: Keep going and the planets vanish entirely. The Sun becomes one star among many, and the nearest of those is 7,000 times further away than Neptune.

lines.text: That’s the Solar System: a few specks of rock and gas, and an enormous amount of nothing.
lines.spoken: That’s the Solar System: a few specks of rock and gas, and an enormous amount of nothing.

lines.text: From 2,000 AU the Sun is just a bright star, and the Milky Way is the real view.
lines.spoken: From 2,000 astronomical units the Sun is just a bright star, and the Milky Way is the real view.

lines.text: This is about what a small telescope shows: Jupiter as a little disc, and four bright dots near it, more or less in a line. Galileo’s telescope was no better than this.
lines.spoken: This is about what a small telescope shows: Jupiter as a little disc, and four bright dots near it, more or less in a line. Galileo’s telescope was no better than this.

lines.text: The clock runs at an hour every second. Keep watching Io, the closest moon. It’s the fastest, and it goes round in under two days.
lines.spoken: The clock runs at an hour every second. Keep watching Io, the closest moon. It’s the fastest, and it goes round in under two days.

lines.text: Now a day every second, like checking back each night. The dots slide from one side to the other and back, always staying close to Jupiter.
lines.spoken: Now a day every second, like checking back each night. The dots slide from one side to the other and back, always staying close to Jupiter.

lines.text: Sometimes a moon vanishes behind Jupiter, or crosses in front of it. Galileo noticed that too. He’d be looking at three dots one night and four the next.
lines.spoken: Sometimes a moon vanishes behind Jupiter, or crosses in front of it. Galileo noticed that too. He’d be looking at three dots one night and four the next.

lines.text: He realised he was watching moons going round another world. Nothing about that fitted the idea that everything circles the Earth.
lines.spoken: He realised he was watching moons going round another world. Nothing about that fitted the idea that everything circles the Earth.

lines.text: The same moons from above Jupiter’s north pole. Now you can see they’re going round in circles.
lines.spoken: The same moons from above Jupiter’s north pole. Now you can see they’re going round in circles.

lines.text: Jupiter from 260,000 kilometres, with the Sun behind us and a little to one side. Those stripes are bands of cloud, and the planet is more than 11 Earths wide.
lines.spoken: Jupiter from 260,000 kilometres, with the Sun behind us and a little to one side. Those stripes are bands of cloud, and the planet is more than 11 Earths wide.

lines.text: The clock runs at 10 minutes every second. Even at this speed you can see Jupiter turning. A whole day here is under ten hours.
lines.spoken: The clock runs at 10 minutes every second. Even at this speed you can see Jupiter turning. A whole day here is under ten hours.

lines.text: There’s Io’s shadow, a small black dot on the clouds. Io itself is out of shot, between Jupiter and the Sun, behind us.
lines.spoken: There’s Io’s shadow, a small black dot on the clouds. Io itself is out of shot, between Jupiter and the Sun, behind us.

lines.text: If you could float in the clouds under that dot, you’d see Io cover the Sun completely. A total eclipse, which happens on Jupiter almost every day.
lines.spoken: If you could float in the clouds under that dot, you’d see Io cover the Sun completely. A total eclipse, which happens on Jupiter almost every day.

lines.text: And here comes Europa’s shadow, close behind. Europa is further out, so it moves more slowly, and its shadow is a little bigger.
lines.spoken: And here comes Europa’s shadow, close behind. Europa is further out, so it moves more slowly, and its shadow is a little bigger.

lines.text: Each shadow takes a couple of hours to cross. With a good telescope, you can watch it happen from your garden.
lines.spoken: Each shadow takes a couple of hours to cross. With a good telescope, you can watch it happen from your garden.

lines.text: An hour a second. Jupiter turns once every 9 hours 56 minutes.
lines.spoken: An hour a second. Jupiter turns once every 9 hours 56 minutes.

lines.text: The Orion Nebula, 1,344 light-years away. It’s a cloud of glowing gas about 24 light-years across, and it’s making stars right now.
lines.spoken: The Orion Nebula, 1,344 light-years away. It’s a cloud of glowing gas about 24 light-years across, and it’s making stars right now.

lines.text: The bright knot in the middle is the Trapezium, a cluster of stars only about a million years old. Their fierce light has carved a hollow in the cloud and makes the gas glow pink.
lines.spoken: The bright knot in the middle is the Trapezium, a cluster of stars only about a million years old. Their fierce light has carved a hollow in the cloud and makes the gas glow pink.

lines.text: The Eagle Nebula, 5,700 light-years away, home of the Pillars of Creation. Those columns of cold gas are about four light-years tall, and new stars are forming in their tips.
lines.spoken: The Eagle Nebula, 5,700 light-years away, home of the Pillars of Creation. Those columns of cold gas are about four light-years tall, and new stars are forming in their tips.

lines.text: The Pleiades, 444 light-years away. These stars were born together about 100 million years ago, from a cloud like Orion’s. The blue haze is a dust cloud they happen to be passing through.
lines.spoken: The Pleiades, 444 light-years away. These stars were born together about 100 million years ago, from a cloud like Orion’s. The blue haze is a dust cloud they happen to be passing through.

lines.text: Our Sun was born like this, 4.6 billion years ago, probably alongside hundreds of sister stars. They’ve long since drifted apart across the galaxy.
lines.spoken: Our Sun was born like this, 4.6 billion years ago, probably alongside hundreds of sister stars. They’ve long since drifted apart across the galaxy.

lines.text: The Lagoon Nebula, 4,100 light-years away, another busy star nursery split by a lane of dust.
lines.spoken: The Lagoon Nebula, 4,100 light-years away, another busy star nursery split by a lane of dust.

lines.text: The Carina Nebula, 8,500 light-years away, where some of the most massive stars in the galaxy are being born.
lines.spoken: The Carina Nebula, 8,500 light-years away, where some of the most massive stars in the galaxy are being born.

lines.text: Our Sun, 4.6 billion years old and about halfway through its life. In some 5 billion years it will run low on hydrogen and swell into a red giant, big enough to swallow Mercury and Venus.
lines.spoken: Our Sun, 4.6 billion years old and about halfway through its life. In some 5 billion years it will run low on hydrogen and swell into a red giant, big enough to swallow Mercury and Venus.

lines.text: This is what comes after. The Ring Nebula, 2,570 light-years away: a dying Sun-like star has puffed its outer layers off into space. The dot in the middle is what’s left, a white dwarf.
lines.spoken: This is what comes after. The Ring Nebula, 2,570 light-years away: a dying Sun-like star has puffed its outer layers off into space. The dot in the middle is what’s left, a white dwarf.

lines.text: The Helix Nebula is much closer, 655 light-years away. Another star’s last breath. Its gas will drift off and end up in new stars and planets.
lines.spoken: The Helix Nebula is much closer, 655 light-years away. Another star’s last breath. Its gas will drift off and end up in new stars and planets.

lines.text: Heavy stars end far more violently. In 1054, astronomers in China recorded a new star so bright it showed in daylight for three weeks. This is the wreck: the Crab Nebula.
lines.spoken: Heavy stars end far more violently. In 1054, astronomers in China recorded a new star so bright it showed in daylight for three weeks. This is the wreck: the Crab Nebula.

lines.text: At its centre is a pulsar, the crushed core of the star. It’s about 20 kilometres across, heavier than the Sun, and spins 30 times a second.
lines.spoken: At its centre is a pulsar, the crushed core of the star. It’s about 20 kilometres across, heavier than the Sun, and spins 30 times a second.

lines.text: The Veil Nebula is an older blast, thousands of years old and now 120 light-years wide, still sweeping up gas as it spreads.
lines.spoken: The Veil Nebula is an older blast, thousands of years old and now 120 light-years wide, still sweeping up gas as it spreads.

lines.text: The iron in your blood and the calcium in your bones were made inside stars like these, long before the Sun existed.
lines.spoken: The iron in your blood and the calcium in your bones were made inside stars like these, long before the Sun existed.

lines.text: Mars from 14,000 kilometres, with the Sun behind us and a little to one side. It’s about half the width of Earth. The labels mark a few famous places.
lines.spoken: Mars from 14,000 kilometres, with the Sun behind us and a little to one side. It’s about half the width of Earth. The labels mark a few famous places.

lines.text: The clock runs at an hour every second. Mars spins once every 24 hours and 37 minutes, so this is a Martian day in about 25 seconds.
lines.spoken: The clock runs at an hour every second. Mars spins once every 24 hours and 37 minutes, so this is a Martian day in about 25 seconds.

lines.text: Watch for Olympus Mons, a volcano about the size of Poland, and the long scar of Valles Marineris, a canyon that would cross the United States.
lines.spoken: Watch for Olympus Mons, a volcano about the size of Poland, and the long scar of Valles Marineris, a canyon that would cross the United States.

lines.text: The two green labels are where NASA’s rovers are working. Curiosity landed in 2012 and Perseverance in 2021. Both are still driving.
lines.spoken: The two green labels are where NASA’s rovers are working. Curiosity landed in 2012 and Perseverance in 2021. Both are still driving.

lines.text: Now from above the north pole. Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos. Neither is round. Phobos is about 27 km long.
lines.spoken: Now from above the north pole. Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos. Neither is round. Phobos is about 27 kilometres long.

lines.text: Phobos goes round in under 8 hours, faster than Mars turns. So from the ground it rises in the west, crosses the sky in about four hours, and does it all again.
lines.spoken: Phobos goes round in under 8 hours, faster than Mars turns. So from the ground it rises in the west, crosses the sky in about four hours, and does it all again.

lines.text: Phobos is also spiralling slowly inwards. In about 50 million years it will either crash or break up into a ring.
lines.spoken: Phobos is also spiralling slowly inwards. In about 50 million years it will either crash or break up into a ring.

lines.text: Hovering over Olympus Mons. Its base is about 600 km across.
lines.spoken: Hovering over Olympus Mons. Its base is about 600 kilometres across.

lines.text: 30 July 2020, from above the Sun. NASA launched Perseverance that morning. China’s Tianwen-1 and the UAE’s Hope had left a week earlier. All three were using the same window.
lines.spoken: 30 July 2020, from above the Sun. NASA launched Perseverance that morning. China’s Tianwen-1 and the UAE’s Hope had left a week earlier. All three were using the same window.

lines.text: A month every second. Earth is on the inside track and moving faster. The spacecraft are coasting outwards on curved paths, aiming for where Mars will be.
lines.spoken: A month every second. Earth is on the inside track and moving faster. The spacecraft are coasting outwards on curved paths, aiming for where Mars will be.

lines.text: 18 February 2021. Seven months and 470 million kilometres later, Perseverance lands in Jezero crater. Mars has moved a long way round the Sun to meet it.
lines.spoken: 18 February 2021. Seven months and 470 million kilometres later, Perseverance lands in Jezero crater. Mars has moved a long way round the Sun to meet it.

lines.text: Keep going. Earth pulls further and further ahead, until it has gone right round and starts catching Mars up from behind.
lines.spoken: Keep going. Earth pulls further and further ahead, until it has gone right round and starts catching Mars up from behind.

lines.text: September 2022, 26 months after the last window. Earth and Mars are back in nearly the same arrangement. The next window after this opened in late 2024, and the one after that in late 2026.
lines.spoken: September 2022, 26 months after the last window. Earth and Mars are back in nearly the same arrangement. The next window after this opened in late 2024, and the one after that in late 2026.

lines.text: October 2020: Earth and Mars at their closest. The spacecraft launched more than two months before this.
lines.spoken: October 2020: Earth and Mars at their closest. The spacecraft launched more than two months before this.

lines.text: Venus through a telescope in June 2024. It’s on the far side of the Sun from us, more than 250 million kilometres away, so it looks small and almost fully lit.
lines.spoken: Venus through a telescope in June 2024. It’s on the far side of the Sun from us, more than 250 million kilometres away, so it looks small and almost fully lit.

lines.text: Now a month every second. Venus is gaining on Earth along its inside lane. Watch it grow, and watch the lit part shrink.
lines.spoken: Now a month every second. Venus is gaining on Earth along its inside lane. Watch it grow, and watch the lit part shrink.

lines.text: 10 January 2025. Venus is exactly half lit and blazing in the evening sky after sunset. It’s about two and a half times closer than it was in June.
lines.spoken: 10 January 2025. Venus is exactly half lit and blazing in the evening sky after sunset. It’s about two and a half times closer than it was in June.

lines.text: A week a second. Now it closes in fast. The crescent gets thinner and bigger at the same time.
lines.spoken: A week a second. Now it closes in fast. The crescent gets thinner and bigger at the same time.

lines.text: Mid March. A thin crescent, about six times wider than it looked in June. It’s only 43 million kilometres from us now.
lines.spoken: Mid March. A thin crescent, about six times wider than it looked in June. It’s only 43 million kilometres from us now.

lines.text: On 23 March it slipped between us and the Sun. Now it’s back on the other side, a crescent again but lit from the other side, rising before dawn as a morning star.
lines.spoken: On 23 March it slipped between us and the Sun. Now it’s back on the other side, a crescent again but lit from the other side, rising before dawn as a morning star.

lines.text: Galileo watched this same sequence in 1610. It only works if Venus goes round the Sun.
lines.spoken: Galileo watched this same sequence in 1610. It only works if Venus goes round the Sun.

lines.text: June 2024: behind the Sun, far away and nearly full.
lines.spoken: June 2024: behind the Sun, far away and nearly full.

lines.text: Five days before passing between us and the Sun. Big and thin.
lines.spoken: Five days before passing between us and the Sun. Big and thin.

lines.text: The same months from above the Sun. Venus laps Earth on the inside track.
lines.spoken: The same months from above the Sun. Venus laps Earth on the inside track.

lines.text: Mercury from above its north pole. The arrow points at the Sun. Our base camp is on the sunny side, and it’s about midday there.
lines.spoken: Mercury from above its north pole. The arrow points at the Sun. Our base camp is on the sunny side, and it’s about midday there.

lines.text: A week every second. Mercury is racing round the Sun, so the arrow swings round with it. The planet is spinning too, just slowly.
lines.spoken: A week every second. Mercury is racing round the Sun, so the arrow swings round with it. The planet is spinning too, just slowly.

lines.text: About four weeks after noon, base camp reaches the line between day and night. The Sun is setting.
lines.spoken: About four weeks after noon, base camp reaches the line between day and night. The Sun is setting.

lines.text: Look: the night side seems to stall for a while. Mercury is near its closest point to the Sun, moving so fast in its orbit that it almost keeps pace with its own spin.
lines.spoken: Look: the night side seems to stall for a while. Mercury is near its closest point to the Sun, moving so fast in its orbit that it almost keeps pace with its own spin.

lines.text: Midnight. Mercury has now been all the way round the Sun once, a whole Mercury year, and base camp has only had half a day.
lines.spoken: Midnight. Mercury has now been all the way round the Sun once, a whole Mercury year, and base camp has only had half a day.

lines.text: Sunrise at last. The night lasted about 88 Earth days and got down to around minus 170 °C.
lines.spoken: Sunrise at last. The night lasted about 88 Earth days and got down to around minus 170 degreesC.

lines.text: And midday again. One day on Mercury, noon to noon, takes 176 Earth days. That’s two of its years.
lines.spoken: And midday again. One day on Mercury, noon to noon, takes 176 Earth days. That’s two of its years.

lines.text: Faster. Count the orbits for each sunrise: two.
lines.spoken: Faster. Count the orbits for each sunrise: two.

lines.text: Venus from above. It spins the opposite way to almost every other planet, once every 243 days.
lines.spoken: Venus from above. It spins the opposite way to almost every other planet, once every 243 days.

lines.text: The Moon at new moon, seen from near Earth. Almost nothing to see — its lit half is pointing away from us, at the Sun.
lines.spoken: The Moon at new moon, seen from near Earth. Almost nothing to see, its lit half is pointing away from us, at the Sun.

lines.text: Now the clock runs at one day every second. Watch the sliver appear and grow.
lines.spoken: Now the clock runs at one day every second. Watch the sliver appear and grow.

lines.text: About a week in: first quarter. Looks like a half-moon, and it is — we’re seeing the lit half exactly side-on.
lines.spoken: About a week in: first quarter. Looks like a half-moon, and it is, we’re seeing the lit half exactly side-on.

lines.text: Waxing gibbous now — more than half, still growing. Each night it rises a little later and looks a little fuller.
lines.spoken: Waxing gibbous now, more than half, still growing. Each night it rises a little later and looks a little fuller.

lines.text: Full moon. The Moon is opposite the Sun, so the whole lit face is turned our way. Nothing about the Moon changed — only our viewing angle.
lines.spoken: Full moon. The Moon is opposite the Sun, so the whole lit face is turned our way. Nothing about the Moon changed, only our viewing angle.

lines.text: And now it shrinks back: waning gibbous, then last quarter, then a thinning crescent on the other side.
lines.spoken: And now it shrinks back: waning gibbous, then last quarter, then a thinning crescent on the other side.

lines.text: Look carefully at the dark part during the crescents — it isn’t quite black. That faint glow is earthshine: sunlight that bounced off Earth and lit the Moon’s night side.
lines.spoken: Look carefully at the dark part during the crescents, it isn’t quite black. That faint glow is earthshine: sunlight that bounced off Earth and lit the Moon’s night side.

lines.text: And back to new moon. 29.5 days, one lap, one full set of phases. That’s a month.
lines.spoken: And back to new moon. 29.5 days, one lap, one full set of phases. That’s a month.

lines.text: Round the back: the face no one on Earth has ever seen from here. Covered in craters, with almost none of the dark “seas”.
lines.spoken: Round the back: the face no one on Earth has ever seen from here. Covered in craters, with almost none of the dark “seas”.

lines.text: Now from above the orbit. Earth in the middle, the Moon on its ring, and the Sun away in the direction of the arrow.
lines.spoken: Now from above the orbit. Earth in the middle, the Moon on its ring, and the Sun away in the direction of the arrow.

lines.text: The Moon is on the same side as the Sun. Its lit half points away from Earth — so from down there, we see a new moon.
lines.spoken: The Moon is on the same side as the Sun. Its lit half points away from Earth, so from down there, we see a new moon.

lines.text: One day a second. Watch the Moon swing round — and notice the lit side of it never changes. It’s always the side facing the Sun.
lines.spoken: One day a second. Watch the Moon swing round, and notice the lit side of it never changes. It’s always the side facing the Sun.

lines.text: A quarter of the way round. From Earth we’re now looking at the lit half edge-on: that’s the first quarter.
lines.spoken: A quarter of the way round. From Earth we’re now looking at the lit half edge-on: that’s the first quarter.

lines.text: Halfway. The Moon is now on the opposite side of Earth from the Sun, so its entire lit face is aimed at us: full moon.
lines.spoken: Halfway. The Moon is now on the opposite side of Earth from the Sun, so its entire lit face is aimed at us: full moon.

lines.text: And round it comes again. One ring, one month, every phase in order — just from the changing angle.
lines.spoken: And round it comes again. One ring, one month, every phase in order, just from the changing angle.

lines.text: Geometry. That’s all a phase has ever been.
lines.spoken: Geometry. That’s all a phase has ever been.

lines.text: The far side of the Moon — tidally locked away from us for billions of years.
lines.spoken: The far side of the Moon, tidally locked away from us for billions of years.

lines.text: Earth in the middle, seen from above the North Pole, and the Moon’s orbit around it. One lap takes 27.3 days.
lines.spoken: Earth in the middle, seen from above the North Pole, and the Moon’s orbit around it. One lap takes 27.3 days.

lines.text: The clock runs at a day every second. Off goes the Moon, anticlockwise, the same way Earth spins.
lines.spoken: The clock runs at a day every second. Off goes the Moon, anticlockwise, the same way Earth spins.

lines.text: Now let’s ride along with the Moon, looking down on it from above. The blue arrow points at Earth. The orange label marks the middle of the side we see.
lines.spoken: Now let’s ride along with the Moon, looking down on it from above. The blue arrow points at Earth. The orange label marks the middle of the side we see.

lines.text: Watch the arrow and the orange label. However far round the Moon goes, the near side stays on Earth’s side.
lines.spoken: Watch the arrow and the orange label. However far round the Moon goes, the near side stays on Earth’s side.

lines.text: Now watch the stars behind. They’re wheeling round. Compared with the distant stars, the Moon is turning, once for every lap.
lines.spoken: Now watch the stars behind. They’re wheeling round. Compared with the distant stars, the Moon is turning, once for every lap.

lines.text: Same speed, same direction: one turn per orbit. That’s tidal locking.
lines.spoken: Same speed, same direction: one turn per orbit. That’s tidal locking.

lines.text: The far side is lit up whenever it faces the Sun. We just never get to see it from here.
lines.spoken: The far side is lit up whenever it faces the Sun. We just never get to see it from here.

lines.text: New moon, 29 January 2025. Seen from the Sun’s side, the far side is in full daylight.
lines.spoken: New moon, 29 January 2025. Seen from the Sun’s side, the far side is in full daylight.

lines.text: Pluto and Charon, a day per second. Each is locked to the other, so they turn together like dancers holding hands, every 6.4 days.
lines.spoken: Pluto and Charon, a day per second. Each is locked to the other, so they turn together like dancers holding hands, every 6.4 days.

lines.text: The Moon through binoculars, two days after new moon. Only a thin crescent is lit, but the labels show where some famous places are.
lines.spoken: The Moon through binoculars, two days after new moon. Only a thin crescent is lit, but the labels show where some famous places are.

lines.text: A day every second. The sunlight creeps across the face, and the labels don’t move at all.
lines.spoken: A day every second. The sunlight creeps across the face, and the labels don’t move at all.

lines.text: First quarter: half lit. The line between day and night runs straight down the middle, and the craters along it cast long shadows.
lines.spoken: First quarter: half lit. The line between day and night runs straight down the middle, and the craters along it cast long shadows.

lines.text: Full moon. Tycho is still near the bottom, Mare Crisium still on the right edge, the Apollo 11 site still in the same spot.
lines.spoken: Full moon. Tycho is still near the bottom, Mare Crisium still on the right edge, the Apollo 11 site still in the same spot.

lines.text: Last quarter. Now the dark creeps in from the other side. Every month for billions of years, the same face.
lines.spoken: Last quarter. Now the dark creeps in from the other side. Every month for billions of years, the same face.

lines.text: New moon again. While the near side goes dark, the far side, out of sight, is in full sunshine.
lines.spoken: New moon again. While the near side goes dark, the far side, out of sight, is in full sunshine.

lines.text: The view changes because of the lighting, not because the Moon is turning to face a different way.
lines.spoken: The view changes because of the lighting, not because the Moon is turning to face a different way.

lines.text: This is Earth. The arrow shows where its sunlight comes from: the Sun is 150 million kilometres away in that direction.
lines.spoken: This is Earth. The arrow shows where its sunlight comes from: the Sun is 150 million kilometres away in that direction.

lines.text: And here it is, from 2.6 million kilometres. You could line up 109 Earths across that disc. The orange marker is pinned to its surface.
lines.spoken: And here it is, from 2.6 million kilometres. You could line up 109 Earths across that disc. The orange marker is pinned to its surface.

lines.text: The clock now runs at a day every second. Keep an eye on the marker. The Sun is turning, just like Earth does, only much more slowly.
lines.spoken: The clock now runs at a day every second. Keep an eye on the marker. The Sun is turning, just like Earth does, only much more slowly.

lines.text: At its equator the Sun goes round about once every 25 days. The real Sun is gas, so its poles lag behind and take about 35. Here it turns in one piece to keep things simple.
lines.spoken: At its equator the Sun goes round about once every 25 days. The real Sun is gas, so its poles lag behind and take about 35. Here it turns in one piece to keep things simple.

lines.text: A week a second now. In 1612 Galileo noticed dark sunspots drifting across the Sun from day to day, and realised the Sun must be spinning.
lines.spoken: A week a second now. In 1612 Galileo noticed dark sunspots drifting across the Sun from day to day, and realised the Sun must be spinning.

lines.text: The light leaving the Sun right now will reach Earth in 8 minutes and 20 seconds.
lines.spoken: The light leaving the Sun right now will reach Earth in 8 minutes and 20 seconds.

lines.text: Half a million kilometres from the surface. The Sun fills the view.
lines.spoken: Half a million kilometres from the surface. The Sun fills the view.

lines.text: The Sun from Mercury, the closest planet. The zoom stays exactly the same for the whole scene. From here the Sun looks almost three times as wide as it does from Earth.

lines.text: From Venus it’s still bigger than we’re used to. Not that anyone standing on Venus could tell. Its clouds never part.

lines.text: This is the Sun as we see it, about half a degree across. That’s roughly half the width of your little finger held out at arm’s length.

lines.text: From Mars, a bit smaller. Sunlight there is less than half as strong as it is here, which is one reason Mars is so cold.

lines.text: From Jupiter the Sun shrinks to a tiny, dazzling dot, a fifth of the width we see. It gets about one twenty-seventh of our sunlight.

lines.text: And from Neptune, 4.5 billion kilometres out, it looks like the brightest star in the sky. It still outshines our full Moon a few hundred times over.

lines.text: Same Sun every time. Only the distance changed.

lines.text: From Pluto, about 5 billion km out. Noon there is roughly as bright as dusk on Earth.
lines.spoken: From Pluto, about 5 billion kilometres out. Noon there is roughly as bright as dusk on Earth.

lines.text: Looking straight down on the Solar System. The Sun in the middle, and the four rocky planets on their rings: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars.
lines.spoken: Looking straight down on the Solar System. The Sun in the middle, and the four rocky planets on their rings: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars.

lines.text: One month every second. Keep your eye on Mercury, closest in — it is already pulling away.

lines.text: That’s roughly a year gone. Earth has done one full lap. Mercury has done more than four.
lines.spoken: That’s roughly a year gone. Earth has done one full lap. Mercury has done more than four.

lines.spoken: Mars is still labouring round its first circuit. It has nearly twice as far to go as Earth, and it’s travelling more slowly: 24 kilometres per second against our 30.

lines.text: Watch Earth catch Mars up and sweep past on the inside. That happens about every 26 months — and it’s when Mars looks biggest and brightest in our sky.
lines.spoken: Watch Earth catch Mars up and sweep past on the inside. That happens about every 26 months, and it’s when Mars looks biggest and brightest in our sky.

lines.text: Closer in means faster and shorter. Both effects pull the same way, which is why the years stretch so dramatically as you go out.

lines.text: August 2003: Earth sweeping past Mars on the inside, closer than at any time in 60,000 years.

lines.text: The same motion seen from Earth, with Mars kept in frame.
lines.spoken: The same motion seen from Earth, with Mars kept in frame.

lines.text: February 2025: every planet from Mercury to Neptune on the same side of the sky at once.

lines.text: Now zoomed right out. The four rocky planets are squashed into that bright knot in the middle — the giants need all this room.

lines.text: Twelve seconds, one Jupiter year. Anyone born on Jupiter would have their first birthday aged nearly twelve.

lines.text: Saturn is less than twice as far out as Jupiter, but its year is nearly three times longer. That is Kepler’s law doing its work.

lines.text: And out at the edge, Uranus and Neptune have barely shifted. Neptune has completed one single orbit since it was discovered in 1846.
lines.spoken: And out at the edge, Uranus and Neptune have barely shifted. Neptune has completed one single orbit since it was discovered in 1846.

lines.text: Distance cubed equals year squared. One line, and it governs everything orbiting the Sun.

lines.text: December 2020: Jupiter catching Saturn. From Earth they appeared 0.1° apart — the closest since 1623.

lines.text: Neptune: 4.5 billion km out, where sunlight is 900 times fainter than here.

lines.text: Saturn in October 2017, as a good telescope would show it. The rings are tipped towards us about as far as they ever get, and we’re looking down on their north side.

lines.text: 23 March 2025. The rings are exactly edge-on to Earth, and they’ve all but vanished. Nobody saw this moment, though. Saturn was right next to the Sun in our sky that month.
lines.spoken: 23 March 2025. The rings are exactly edge-on to Earth, and they’ve all but vanished. Nobody saw this moment, though. Saturn was right next to the Sun in our sky that month.

lines.text: Around 2032 they’ll be wide open again. The whole cycle, from open to edge-on and round again, takes one Saturn year: 29 and a half Earth years.
lines.spoken: Around 2032 they’ll be wide open again. The whole cycle, from open to edge-on and round again, takes one Saturn year: 29 and a half Earth years.

lines.text: Here’s Saturn up close, at an hour per second. You can see the rings’ shadow on the planet, and the gaps between the rings, swept clear by the gravity of Saturn’s moons.
lines.spoken: Here’s Saturn up close, at an hour per second. You can see the rings’ shadow on the planet, and the gaps between the rings, swept clear by the gravity of Saturn’s moons.

lines.text: March 2025: edge-on. The rings are about 10 metres thick, so they almost disappear.
lines.spoken: March 2025: edge-on. The rings are about 10 metres thick, so they almost disappear.

lines.text: Uranus as seen from the Sun, in January 1986, when Voyager 2 flew past. Its south pole is pointing almost straight at us, and at the Sun. The thin hoops are its rings.
lines.spoken: Uranus as seen from the Sun, in January 1986, when Voyager 2 flew past. Its south pole is pointing almost straight at us, and at the Sun. The thin hoops are its rings.

lines.text: December 2007, a quarter of the way round its 84-year orbit. Now we’re looking at the equator. The axis lies almost flat, and the rings stand on end.
lines.spoken: December 2007, a quarter of the way round its 84-year orbit. Now we’re looking at the equator. The axis lies almost flat, and the rings stand on end.

lines.text: A year every second. Watch the planet’s north pole slowly swing round to face the Sun, while the planet itself spins once every 17 hours.
lines.spoken: A year every second. Watch the planet’s north pole slowly swing round to face the Sun, while the planet itself spins once every 17 hours.

lines.text: Remember that the tilt isn’t changing. Uranus is moving round the Sun, and we’re watching from the Sun, so we see it from a different side.
lines.spoken: Remember that the tilt isn’t changing. Uranus is moving round the Sun, and we’re watching from the Sun, so we see it from a different side.

lines.text: Around 2030 the north pole points at the Sun. Up there it’s the middle of a summer that lasts about 21 years, and the Sun hasn’t set since 2007.
lines.spoken: Around 2030 the north pole points at the Sun. Up there it’s the middle of a summer that lasts about 21 years, and the Sun hasn’t set since 2007.

lines.text: Now Neptune, from above, a day per second. Its big moon Triton is going round the opposite way to Neptune’s spin. No other big moon does that.
lines.spoken: Now Neptune, from above, a day per second. Its big moon Triton is going round the opposite way to Neptune’s spin. No other big moon does that.

lines.text: Triton is probably a dwarf planet that wandered too close and got captured. It’s slowly spiralling inwards, and in a few billion years Neptune will tear it apart.
lines.spoken: Triton is probably a dwarf planet that wandered too close and got captured. It’s slowly spiralling inwards, and in a few billion years Neptune will tear it apart.

lines.text: Equinox: the Sun is over Uranus’s equator. An hour a second shows its 17-hour spin.
lines.spoken: Equinox: the Sun is over Uranus’s equator. An hour a second shows its 17-hour spin.

lines.where: uranus jump "Uranus from above the Sun"
lines.text: Its 84-year orbit, from above. At a year per second it takes about a minute and a half to go round.
lines.spoken: Its 84-year orbit, from above. At a year per second it takes about a minute and a half to go round.

lines.text: The June solstice. The blue dashed line is Earth’s axis, and the arrow points at the Sun. Look how the north end of the axis is leaning towards it.
lines.spoken: The June solstice. The blue dashed line is Earth’s axis, and the arrow points at the Sun. Look how the north end of the axis is leaning towards it.

lines.text: That’s why the whole Arctic is bathed in light, and why northern countries get their longest day right now.
lines.spoken: That’s why the whole Arctic is bathed in light, and why northern countries get their longest day right now.

lines.text: Three months on, the September equinox. The tilt hasn’t changed — but now it’s sideways-on to the Sun, so neither pole is favoured.
lines.spoken: Three months on, the September equinox. The tilt hasn’t changed, but now it’s sideways-on to the Sun, so neither pole is favoured.

lines.text: Notice the line between day and night runs straight through both poles. Twelve hours of each, almost everywhere on Earth.
lines.spoken: Notice the line between day and night runs straight through both poles. Twelve hours of each, almost everywhere on Earth.

lines.text: The December solstice. Same tilt, same direction in space — but Earth has gone round to the other side of the Sun, so now the north leans away.
lines.spoken: The December solstice. Same tilt, same direction in space, but Earth has gone round to the other side of the Sun, so now the north leans away.

lines.text: The Arctic is in darkness and Antarctica is in constant daylight. Opposite seasons, at the same instant, on one planet.
lines.spoken: The Arctic is in darkness and Antarctica is in constant daylight. Opposite seasons, at the same instant, on one planet.

lines.text: The March equinox, and we’re balanced again on the way back round.
lines.spoken: The March equinox, and we’re balanced again on the way back round.

lines.text: And back to June. One lap of the Sun, one full set of seasons — and the axis pointed the same way the entire time.
lines.spoken: And back to June. One lap of the Sun, one full set of seasons, and the axis pointed the same way the entire time.

lines.where: yearrun jump "Look down from the north"
lines.text: From above: in December, the North Pole is in darkness no matter how Earth turns.
lines.spoken: From above: in December, the North Pole is in darkness no matter how Earth turns.

lines.text: Zoomed right out: Earth’s near-circular lap of the Sun, one month every second.
lines.spoken: Zoomed right out: Earth’s near-circular lap of the Sun, one month every second.

lines.text: We’re above Svalbard, at 78° north — well inside the Arctic Circle — at midnight on the June solstice. And it’s broad daylight.
lines.spoken: We’re above Svalbard, at 78 degrees north, well inside the Arctic Circle, at midnight on the June solstice. And it’s broad daylight.

lines.text: An hour a second. Watch the ground turn beneath us — and watch for a sunset that never comes.
lines.spoken: An hour a second. Watch the ground turn beneath us, and watch for a sunset that never comes.

lines.text: Six hours in. Still light. The Sun is just sliding round the sky, low in the north, instead of dipping below the horizon.
lines.spoken: Six hours in. Still light. The Sun is just sliding round the sky, low in the north, instead of dipping below the horizon.

lines.text: A whole rotation, and this spot has never once entered the dark half. That’s the midnight Sun.
lines.spoken: A whole rotation, and this spot has never once entered the dark half. That’s the midnight Sun.

lines.text: Now jump to the December solstice, same place. Earth is on the other side of the Sun, the north leans away — and now the Sun never rises.
lines.spoken: Now jump to the December solstice, same place. Earth is on the other side of the Sun, the north leans away, and now the Sun never rises.

lines.text: Months of daylight, then months of darkness. All from a 23.4° lean.
lines.spoken: Months of daylight, then months of darkness. All from a 23.4 degrees lean.

lines.text: The opposite end of the planet, on the same date: endless daylight over Antarctica.
lines.spoken: The opposite end of the planet, on the same date: endless daylight over Antarctica.

lines.text: On the equator the day is about twelve hours long on every date of the year — no real seasons at all.
lines.spoken: On the equator the day is about twelve hours long on every date of the year, no real seasons at all.

lines.text: We’re looking at Earth from the direction of the Sun, so the stars behind it are the ones you’d see from Earth at midnight. In December that means Orion, Taurus and Gemini.
lines.spoken: We’re looking at Earth from the direction of the Sun, so the stars behind it are the ones you’d see from Earth at midnight. In December that means Orion, Taurus and Gemini.

lines.text: Now the clock runs at a month every second. Earth heads round the Sun, and the view behind it slides along.
lines.spoken: Now the clock runs at a month every second. Earth heads round the Sun, and the view behind it slides along.

lines.text: June. Now Scorpius and Sagittarius are behind Earth, with the bright heart of the Milky Way. Orion is on the other side of the Sun, up in the daytime where we can’t see him.
lines.spoken: June. Now Scorpius and Sagittarius are behind Earth, with the bright heart of the Milky Way. Orion is on the other side of the Sun, up in the daytime where we can’t see him.

lines.text: Keep going, through the autumn constellations, Pegasus and Pisces, and round towards December again.
lines.spoken: Keep going, through the autumn constellations, Pegasus and Pisces, and round towards December again.

lines.text: And back to Orion. One trip round the Sun, one full turn of the night sky.
lines.spoken: And back to Orion. One trip round the Sun, one full turn of the night sky.

lines.text: March: Leo and Virgo at midnight.
lines.spoken: March: Leo and Virgo at midnight.

lines.text: September: Pegasus and Aquarius.
lines.spoken: September: Pegasus and Aquarius.

lines.text: Now we’re on Earth looking at the Sun, with the daytime sky switched off so the stars show. On 20 March the Sun sits in front of Pisces.
lines.spoken: Now we’re on Earth looking at the Sun, with the daytime sky switched off so the stars show. On 20 March the Sun sits in front of Pisces.

lines.text: A week every second. The Sun creeps steadily eastwards against the stars, about two of its own widths every day.
lines.spoken: A week every second. The Sun creeps steadily eastwards against the stars, about two of its own widths every day.

lines.text: A month a second: a year in twelve seconds. The line the Sun follows is the ecliptic, and the constellations along it are the zodiac.
lines.spoken: A month a second: a year in twelve seconds. The line the Sun follows is the ecliptic, and the constellations along it are the zodiac.

lines.text: Early December. The Sun is between Scorpius and Sagittarius, in a patch of sky that officially belongs to Ophiuchus, the serpent bearer. No horoscope mentions it.
lines.spoken: Early December. The Sun is between Scorpius and Sagittarius, in a patch of sky that officially belongs to Ophiuchus, the serpent bearer. No horoscope mentions it.

lines.text: On through Sagittarius, Capricornus and Aquarius.
lines.spoken: On through Sagittarius, Capricornus and Aquarius.

lines.text: And back to Pisces. Thirteen constellations, one year.
lines.spoken: And back to Pisces. Thirteen constellations, one year.

lines.text: Mid July, and the clock is running at a week a second. Pause it when it reaches your birthday to see which constellation the Sun is really in.
lines.spoken: Mid July, and the clock is running at a week a second. Pause it when it reaches your birthday to see which constellation the Sun is really in.
